query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minor amount of a high‐melting, ductile microalloying element (such as approximately 2–4 at.% Nb) into (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 will promote the in‐situ formation of a ductile, Nb‐rich intergranular phase that strengthens grain boundaries. This microstructural modification will enhance the compressive integrity and crack‐resistance of the alloy without degrading its large caloric response.
generation.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy that exhibits a large caloric effect under applied-field/pressure-field operation but suffers from poor mechanical integrity and a tendency to crack.
generation.intervention: Microalloy the base alloy by adding a controlled 2–4 at.% of Nb during synthesis so that Nb segregates to grain boundaries and forms a fine, ductile Nb-rich second phase in situ.
generation.conditions: Samples are processed under the same casting/sintering conditions as the baseline alloy and are then subjected to identical applied-field or pressure-field caloric cycling, temperature cycling, and compressive loading conditions as previously reported.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a discontinuous, Nb-rich ductile intergranular phase that bridges grain boundaries and impedes crack initiation and propagation.
generation.mechanism: Nb addition is expected to preferentially segregate to grain boundaries during solidification, lowering the local melting point and promoting the precipitation of a ductile phase. This phase acts to reinforce grain boundaries and arrest crack propagation. Because the main caloric phase transition in the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 matrix remains dominant, the caloric response is preserved while mechanical integrity (compressive strength and toughness) is enhanced.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified alloy, the Nb-microalloyed variant should exhibit a higher compressive strength (targeting improvements, for example, from values near 150–220 MPa to significantly higher levels) and reduced crack propagation under load. At the same time, caloric performance metrics (e.g., entropy change under field/pressure) should remain largely unchanged.
generation.baseline: The original (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy with excellent caloric response but poor mechanical integrity (evidenced by low compressive strength and proneness to cracking).
generation.boundary: All tests are performed under the same applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes as in prior studies on MM′X materials; the alloy remains rare-earth-free.
generation.uncertainty: It is uncertain how sensitive the caloric phase transition is to Nb-induced modifications; the optimal Nb concentration and its effect on the caloric response must be experimentally calibrated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy with a 2–4 at.% Nb addition and one set of control samples without Nb. Subject both sets to identical processing and then test them under the same applied magnetic/pressure fields, temperature cycles, and compressive loading conditions.
measurements: Measure compressive strength and assess crack propagation (using microscopy and fracture analysis).
Quantify the caloric response (e.g., entropy change and adiabatic temperature change) under identical field/pressure cycling.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-added samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in mechanical integrity (higher compressive strength and reduced cracking) or if their caloric response is notably reduced compared to the control samples, the hypothesis is falsified.
